A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SzCORE challenge, retaining the original algorithms and Filadelfia cohort despite the changed title. The main text, figures, tables, and appendices A–C in v1 and A–E in v2 are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 28 submissions on 65 patients, including seizure-detection scores, algorithm agreement, and computational resource measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains the original benchmark evaluation and adds cross-dataset results, patient-level statistical comparisons, and seizure- and patient-level failure analyses.

M1.justification: The evaluated architectures, preprocessing, windowing, and postprocessing remain unchanged in Section 5 and Appendix A, Table 2. The expanded benchmarking and statistical analyses do not introduce a new seizure-detection method.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands beyond Filadelfia to Siena, TUH Seizure Corpus, and SeizeIT1, covering additional curated recordings and continuous EMU data (Appendix D, Table 6). Siena and TUH previously appeared as training resources. CHB-MIT evaluation was attempted but produced no scores because of montage incompatibility; training coverage in Table 3 is unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same 28 submissions. Names such as Sz Transformer/SeizureTransformer and Gradient Boost/Multi-scale Gradient Boosting refer to retained methods. The additional dataset evaluations use an existing open-source subset without introducing new comparator methods.

E3.justification: The added cross-dataset protocol restricts evaluation to open-source submissions, includes TUH train/dev/eval subsets, and excludes methods trained on the target dataset from rank correlations. The original Filadelfia cohort, scoring tolerances, and subjectwise averaging remain unchanged as stated; the newly disclosed zero-precision convention does not establish a change in prior execution.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained agreement and self-report comparisons, v2 adds rank-versus-F1 analysis, seizure-duration and day/night failure comparisons, simultaneous failures across the top five algorithms, and cross-dataset ranking analysis. Section 6 and Appendix D therefore substantially expand investigation of patient-level failures and generalization.

E5.justification: v1 provides descriptive comparisons without inferential testing. v2 adds Friedman testing, Wilcoxon comparisons with Holm-Bonferroni correction, Nemenyi comparisons, Cliff's delta effect sizes, and Spearman rank correlations (Section 4 and Tables 5 and 7). These are new statistical analyses, without a reported increase in repeated runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Table 1 substantially revises F1 and precision: Sz Transformer changes from 43%/45% to 32%/29%, while sensitivity remains 37%. DeepSOZ-HEM moves above S4Seizure v2. Tables 5–7 add cross-dataset and statistical outcomes, and Section 6 newly reports simultaneous top-five failures for 15/65 patients. The cause of the original-score revisions is not fully explained.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical propositions, proofs, or derivations. The added statistical tests and empirical ranking analyses do not introduce a theoretical contribution.

C1.justification: The generalization-gap and continuing-benchmark claims are retained, but v2 adds a prominent abstract-level claim that highest aggregate F1 does not imply population-level stability and may conceal failures on outlier patients. This introduces a distinct central reliability contribution beyond v1's challenge-performance report.

C2.justification: v2 proposes short seizure duration and processing windows as failure explanations, links ranking discordance to patient-level variability, and interprets cross-dataset differences through curation bias. Appendix D adds the montage-compatibility limitation, while the new Impact Statement discusses clinical risks from patient-specific failures and underrepresented populations.

D1.justification: v2 adds access instructions for algorithm information and GitHub pull-request submissions, identifies additional dataset versions, and specifies setting undefined subject precision to zero when averaging. It removes v1's explicit 19-channel ordering. Hardware specifications and the implementation and resource details in Tables 2–4 are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting statistical comparisons, SeizeIT1, the EEG montage, and SeizureTransformer, including Demšar (2006) and Wu et al. (2025). The broader positioning against existing reviews, earlier challenges, and commercial systems remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and substantial portions of the introduction, algorithm-collection description, and evaluation narrative are rewritten around an empirical generalization study. Section names change, and an Impact Statement and two analytical appendices extend the document structure, although much of the discussion and conclusion is retained.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main document from one to two columns, redraws Figure 2, removes Table 1's score shading, and adds two statistical figures and Tables 5–7. The original agreement and self-report plots are retained as Figures 5–6. Appendix placement also changes, including an isolated Appendix A heading before its table.

improvement.justification: v2 improves v1's largely descriptive benchmark through statistical comparisons, failure analyses, additional dataset results, and clearer scoring and access information. However, reporting inconsistencies limit these gains: Table 5's correlation counts of 13/14 are unexplained alongside Table 6's ten methods, and Figure 6 retains the earlier score positions despite Table 1's revisions. The added evidence is useful, but its incomplete reconciliation limits the overall improvement.
